name: Giggs Hill Green
text: Your train passes near Giggs Hill Green in Thames Ditton, on the train's {side}, a triangular green where the village has played cricket since 1833. Despite its name, there is no hill.

name: Hampton Court Palace
text: Your train passes near Hampton Court Palace, on the train's {side}. Building began in 1514 for Cardinal Wolsey, who gave it to Henry VIII in 1529; in the 1690s William III rebuilt much of it to rival the Palace of Versailles.

name: Ashtead Common
text: Your train passes near Ashtead Common, on the train's {side}, a wood with more than 2,300 pollarded oaks, many of them 300 to 400 years old. It belongs to the City of London, and much of it is a National Nature Reserve.

name: Epsom
text: Your train passes through Epsom, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. In the late 17th century a spring on Epsom Common was thought to heal, and its water was rich in what became known as Epsom salts.

name: Bugby Chapel
text: Your train passes near Bugby Chapel in Epsom, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 by a Calvinist preacher, William Bugby. It was later a Baptist chapel and, from 1954, a synagogue; since 1994 it has been an office.

name: Laine Theatre Arts
text: Your train passes Laine Theatre Arts in Epsom, on the train's {side}, a college for dance and musical theatre founded in 1974 by the dancer Betty Laine. Victoria Beckham trained there.

name: Nonsuch Palace
text: Your train passes near the site of Nonsuch Palace, on the train's {side}, begun by Henry VIII in 1538 to rival the French king's Château de Chambord. It was pulled down in 1682 and 1683 by Barbara, Countess of Castlemaine, who sold the materials to pay her gambling debts.

name: Fitznells Manor
text: Your train passes near Fitznells Manor in Ewell, on the train's {side}, the last surviving manor house in the borough of Epsom and Ewell. Its oldest part is a wing of a timber-framed hall house probably built in the early 16th century.

name: The Beehive, Gatwick Airport
text: Your train passes near the Beehive, on the train's {side}, Gatwick's first terminal: a round building opened in 1936, when passengers came by fast train from London Victoria to fly to Paris. It is now offices.

name: East Chiltington
text: Your train passes near East Chiltington, on the train's {side}, a village whose church is 13th century in origin. A Roman road, the Sussex Greensand Way, runs through the middle of its parish.

name: Lewes Castle
text: Your train passes near Lewes Castle, on the train's {side}, built by William de Warenne after the Norman Conquest. Unusually it has two mottes, or mounds; the only other castle in England like it is Lincoln Castle.

name: Falmer Stadium
text: Your train passes near Falmer Stadium, known as the Amex, on the train's {side}: home of Brighton & Hove Albion since 2011, with room for 32,500. It has also held matches in the 2015 Rugby World Cup and the Women's Euro 2022.

name: Moulsecoomb Place
text: Your train passes near Moulsecoomb Place, on the train's {side}, a farmhouse remodelled as a Neoclassical mansion in 1790. The council bought it between the wars, when Moulsecoomb became a large council estate, and it later became part of the University of Brighton.

name: Brighton Toy and Model Museum
text: Your train passes near the Brighton Toy and Model Museum, on the train's {side}, which fills four Victorian arches under the forecourt of Brighton station. Founded in 1991, it holds more than 10,000 toys and models.

name: Lewes Priory
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Lewes Priory, on the train's {side}, the first Cluniac priory in England. In 1264, after losing the Battle of Lewes, Henry III retreated there and was forced to accept a council that marked the start of parliamentary government in England.

name: Mount Caburn
text: Your train passes near Mount Caburn, on the train's {side}, a 150-metre hill with an Iron Age hill fort on top. It has been dug so often, with 170 trenches, that it may have had more excavations than any other site in Britain.

name: Glynde Place
text: Your train passes near Glynde Place, on the train's {side}, an Elizabethan manor house built in 1569 and still the family home of the Viscounts Hampden. Since 2013 its grounds have held the Love Supreme Jazz Festival every summer.

name: Ovenden's Mill, Polegate
text: Your train passes near Ovenden's Mill in Polegate, on the train's {side}, a four-storey brick tower mill built in 1817. It worked by wind until 1943, and then by engine until 1965.

name: Hampden Park
text: Your train passes through Hampden Park, a suburb of Eastbourne on the train's {side}. Trains on the East Coastway Line often pass through its station twice, and its level crossing is thought to be one of the busiest in Europe.

name: Stone Cross Windmill
text: Your train passes near Stone Cross Windmill, on the train's {side}, built in 1876 and worked by wind until 1937. It was a lookout post in the Second World War, and after a long restoration it was making wholemeal flour again in 2000.

name: Eastbourne
text: Your train passes through Eastbourne, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. The seaside resort lies just east of Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in Great Britain.

name: Pevensey Castle
text: Your train passes near Pevensey Castle, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort called Anderitum built around 290 AD. The Normans reoccupied it in 1066 and built a castle inside its walls; it was besieged several times but never taken by storm.

name: St Nicolas' Church, Pevensey
text: Your train passes near St Nicolas' Church in Pevensey, on the train's {side}, built between 1205 and 1216 and named after the patron saint of seafarers. Its size reflects Pevensey's importance as a seaport then; the sea is now about half a mile away.

name: Normans Bay
text: Your train passes Normans Bay, a coastal hamlet on the train's {side}, called Pevensey Sluice until the railway halt opened in 1905. In 2005 divers found cannons offshore, perhaps from a Dutch warship sunk in the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690.

name: Gillham Wood
text: Your train passes Gillham Wood, on the train's {side}, a Sussex Wildlife Trust reserve of oak with hazel, birch and holly. An old bomb crater in it is now a pond, and 74 kinds of bird have been recorded there.

name: De La Warr Pavilion
text: Your train passes near the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, on the train's {side}, built in 1935 and described by Historic England as the UK's first public building in the Modernist style. Since 2005 it has been an arts centre.

name: SM UB-131
text: Your train passes near Bulverhythe, on the train's {side}, where a German submarine from the First World War, UB-131, was wrecked in January 1921 while being towed from Harwich to Falmouth for explosive trials. The wreck was sold for £655 and broken up where it lay.

name: St Leonards West Marina station
text: Your train passes near the site of St Leonards West Marina station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1846 and caught up in a feud between two rival railway companies over the way into Hastings. It closed in 1967.

name: Senlac Hill
text: Your train passes near Senlac Hill, on the train's {side}, where Harold is generally thought to have placed his army for the Battle of Hastings on October 14th 1066. Battle Abbey was later built on top of it.

name: Glottenham Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Glottenham Castle, on the train's {side}, built in the late 13th century with stone walls, two square towers and a gatehouse. It belonged to the de Etchingham family and was abandoned by the 17th century.

name: Robertsbridge
text: Your train passes Robertsbridge, on the train's {side}, a village thought to date from 1176, when a Cistercian abbey was founded there. A 14th-century manuscript found here, the Robertsbridge Codex, holds the earliest surviving music written for keyboard.

name: Etchingham church
text: Your train passes near Etchingham's 14th-century church, on the train's {side}, whose spire carries what is probably England's oldest brass weather vane. The village's medieval manor house stood where the railway now runs.

name: Wadhurst Castle
text: Your train passes near Wadhurst Castle, on the train's {side}, a castle-style mansion first built between 1818 and 1820 and remodelled for Benjamin Harding, who bought it in 1838. It is now a wedding venue.

name: The Pantiles
text: Your train passes near the Pantiles in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, a Georgian colonnade leading from the iron-rich spring, found in 1606, that gave the town its name. In summer, costumed 'dippers' serve the water to visitors.

name: Trinity Theatre
text: Your train passes near Trinity Theatre in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, which was Holy Trinity Church from 1829 to 1972. Decimus Burton designed it, in sandstone from Calverley Quarry; it is now a theatre and arts centre.

name: Tonbridge Castle
text: Your train passes near Tonbridge Castle, on the train's {side}, first built after the Norman Conquest to guard the crossing of the River Medway. Its twin-towered gatehouse took 30 years to build and was finished in 1260.

name: Haysden Country Park
text: Your train passes Haysden Country Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1988 on the edge of Tonbridge. It has two lakes, Barden Lake and Haysden Water, and the River Medway runs through it.

name: Stoneleigh station
text: Stoneleigh station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1932. It is in London fare zone 5, and is the only National Rail station in that zone that isn't in a London borough.

name: Frant station
text: Frant station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1851. It stands in the hamlet of Bells Yew Green, about two kilometres from the village of Frant itself.

name: The Greenwich meridian
text: Your train crosses the Greenwich meridian on the edge of Lewes, a town that sits on the line of zero longitude. The Greenwich Meridian Trail, a long walk from Peacehaven to East Yorkshire, passes through the middle of the town.
